## Design

### 2026-10-17 – October 17: Late Start, Learning CAD from Scratch & Getting the ESP32 Mount Done!

**5h**

October 17: Late Start, Learning CAD from Scratch & Getting the ESP32 Mount Done!
First off, I’m running a bit behind on this project because school work has been absolutely crazy lately, but we’re finally here and making real progress!

Some people might look at a simple setup like this and say "This shouldn’t take 5 hours to design," but for me, it definitely does because I started with pretty much zero CAD experience. Learning Fusion 360 while trying to build functional hardware parts at the same time is no joke, but honestly, seeing the model come together makes it totally worth it!

1. Keep It Simple: The Core Concept
The idea behind this turret is super clean and straightforward. I'm not using a custom printed PCB for this build—just the raw components hooked together directly with jumper wires:

Brain: ESP32-C3 SuperMini

Actuators: 2x SG90 Micro Servos (pan & tilt)

Payload: 5V Laser Diode module

Power: Directly powered via a single USB-C cable into the ESP32 board.

2. STEP Models & CAD Struggles
To make sure everything actually fits in 3D, I brought the official STEP model of the ESP32-C3 SuperMini into Fusion 360 as a separate component (.f3d). Design-wise, the biggest hurdle was that this tiny board has no mounting holes at all.

Here is how I solved the internal layout:

Pin Clearance (Standoffs): Headers and solder joints stick out about 3–4 mm on the bottom. To stop them from pressing against the casing, I added 4.5 mm corner pillars so the PCB sits elevated with enough breathing room.

USB-C Port: Modeled a custom opening on the outer wall with rounded corners (Fillet) so the cable plugs in smoothly without jamming.

Wall Thickness: Checked my wall tolerances around the screw mounts—originally they were too thin (~1 mm), so I bumped them up to 2 mm so the 3D print doesn't crack under stress.

(Insert screenshot of your Fusion 360 model here)

3. What’s Next & Game Plan for Tomorrow
I have a ton of school stuff to finish for today, so I have to cut this session a bit short, but the baseline is rock solid.

Tomorrow's checklist:

Slightly tweak the ESP32 mount geometry for a tighter fit.

Drop in the 2x SG90 servos and laser module models into the main assembly to double-check that all components clear each other without hitting internal walls.

Finish up the control code and test the pan-tilt motion routines.

Time spent this session: ~5 hours

### 2026-10-18 – ### October 18: Thought I Only Had a Few Minutes Left, But It Turned Into a 5-Hour Code Marathon!

**5h**

### October 18: Thought I Only Had a Few Minutes Left, But It Turned Into a 5-Hour Code Marathon!

I honestly thought today's session was going to be super quick. I figured I only had a tiny bit of code left to wrap up the web server and button handling for the pan-tilt turret, and I would be done in no time. Well... I was completely wrong. What was supposed to be a quick 20-minute polish turned into an intense 5-hour coding marathon!

---

## 1. Tackling the Web Server & Code Logic

Writing code for the ESP32-C3 in Arduino IDE always has its little quirks, especially when you are combining Wi-Fi access points, servo libraries, and web handlers all at once.

Here is what kept me locked in for five hours straight:

* The Web UI Grid: Polishing up the HTML and CSS inside the PROGMEM block so the control layout looks clean on a phone screen. I set up a simple 3x3 grid for the direction arrows and a toggle button for the laser module.
* Server Handlers & AJAX: Writing the handleMove and handleLaser routes so the browser can send asynchronous fetch requests without constantly reloading the entire page. Every time you tap an arrow, it adjusts the panAngle or tiltAngle, constrains them safely between 0 and 180 degrees, and updates the live text display on the phone.
* Pin Mapping & Servo Attachments: Making sure the SG90 servos map correctly to GPIO 1 and GPIO 2, and wiring the laser diode logic to GPIO 3 with clean state tracking (HIGH or LOW).

It took a lot of trial, error, and debugging to get the asynchronous JavaScript calls talking smoothly to the ESP32 backend without any lag, but seeing it all come together in the serial monitor was totally worth it.

---

### 2. Wrapping Up & Next Steps

My eyes are tired and my brain is fried after sitting here for 5 hours straight, but the core software side of the laser turret is officially finished and ready for testing as soon as the physical hardware parts arrive in the mail!

Time spent this session: ~5 hours (turns out "a little bit of code" is a lie we always tell ourselves).
